diagrams.title: Find an image using words
diagrams.subtitle: Separate image and text encoders meet at a similarity score
trace: Use the typed query 'a red sports car on a road'.
CIFAR-10 photographs already have image vectors stored in img_emb.
Encode the query once and compare it with every image vector.
Display the six highest-ranked images; inspect whether they match the words.
diagrams.explanation: A modality is a kind of data, such as text or an image. CLIP connects these two modalities through an embedding: a vector describing an input. The image branch prepares photographs and passes them through the image encoder; the text branch tokenizes the query and passes it through the text encoder. Projection layers put both outputs into one shared vector space. Normalisation makes vector length consistent so the dot product measures cosine similarity. Each image receives one score against the query, then ranking selects the highest scores. The gallery can be encoded before a query arrives, which avoids repeating image processing for each search. This lab uses a pretrained, frozen CLIP model. Retrieval changes the query and ranking, rather than training new model weights.
diagrams.check_question: When a new text query arrives, must every gallery image be encoded again?
diagrams.check_answer: No. Reuse stored image embeddings, encode the new query and compare its vector with them.

diagrams.insert_before_title: The contrastive objective as a matrix
diagrams.title: How matching pairs teach CLIP
diagrams.subtitle: Learn which caption belongs to each image, and vice versa

steps.title: Score all pairs
steps.detail: One row and column per pair

diagrams.feedback: In training, loss gradients update encoders; the lab only measures loss.
trace: Imagine three pairs: car with car caption, bird with bird caption, ship with ship caption.
All comparisons form a 3 by 3 score matrix; the correct pairs occupy its diagonal.
The car row should prefer the car caption over the bird and ship captions.
The car-caption column should prefer the car image over the other images.
Compare correct versus shuffled captions in the lab; no optimiser runs here.
diagrams.explanation: Contrastive learning learns a representation by comparing matching and non-matching examples. A batch is a small group of image-caption pairs processed together. After both encoders produce vectors, every image is compared with every caption. If the input lists retain their original pairing, the correct comparisons lie on the diagonal of the matrix. Each row asks which caption belongs to an image; each column asks which image belongs to a caption. Temperature changes how sharply score differences affect the matching probabilities. Cross-entropy measures the error in these choices, and CLIP averages the two directions. In training, backpropagation uses that error to change encoder weights. In this lab the embeddings are frozen: clip_loss demonstrates the objective by comparing correct and shuffled pairs, without performing a training step.
diagrams.check_question: For three matching pairs, how many comparisons are made, and where are the three target pairs?
diagrams.check_answer: Nine comparisons form a 3 by 3 matrix. The three target pairs are on the diagonal.

diagrams.title: Follow the multimodal lab
diagrams.subtitle: Inspect representations before judging search and speech outputs
trace: Inspect img_emb.shape: one row represents one gallery image.
Compare classification accuracy for a class name and for caption-like templates.
If four of five returned pictures have the queried class, precision@5 is 0.8.
Look at both loss values and the PCA plot; neither changes CLIP's weights.
Inspect a Whisper transcript before using it as a CLIP search query.
diagrams.explanation: The notebook first loads labelled photographs; the labels are used to evaluate outputs, rather than train CLIP. The embed_images and embed_texts functions prepare the shared representations reused throughout the lab. The zero_shot_accuracy function compares each image with descriptions of all classes and measures how often the selected class is correct. Retrieval reverses that perspective: a text query ranks the gallery. Despite its historical name, recall_at_k measures the fraction of returned images belonging to the requested class, averaged across class queries: precision at k. The clip_loss function then illustrates the training objective, while PCA compresses vectors into a two-dimensional view for inspection. Finally, Whisper converts speech into words. The wer function evaluates transcription errors before the transcript becomes a text query. Each intermediate output helps locate which stage caused a failure.
diagrams.check_question: Four of five returned images match the query class. What does 4/5 measure in this lab?
diagrams.check_answer: Precision@5: the fraction of returned results that are relevant, rather than the fraction of all relevant gallery images retrieved.

diagrams.title: One contrastive learning step
diagrams.subtitle: CLIP training is explained here; the lab uses fixed encoders
diagrams.explanation: Contrastive training teaches encoders to distinguish matching pairs from non-matching pairs. Each row of a batch contains an image and its own caption. The encoders produce vectors, and every image is compared with every caption to make a square score matrix. The labelled matches lie on the diagonal when the pairing order is preserved. One loss asks each image to choose its caption; another asks each caption to choose its image. Their average supplies the learning signal. In a training system, gradients from this loss update encoder weights. This lab deliberately does not run that update: it uses a pretrained CLIP model and compares the loss for correct and shuffled pairs.
trace: Take three pairs: dog, car and ship, each with its own caption.
There are 3 × 3 = 9 comparisons, with 3 diagonal matches.
If every caption choice has probability 1/3, one loss is −ln(1/3) = ln 3, about 1.10.
A confident correct choice gives lower loss; no training step is performed in the lab.
diagrams.check_question: Is calculating a loss the same as training the model?
diagrams.check_answer: No. Training also needs gradients and an optimiser step to update weights.
diagrams.feedback: Training gradients update encoders; this lab only measures loss.

diagrams.title: Search a gallery using speech
diagrams.subtitle: A speech transcript becomes the text query for CLIP
diagrams.explanation: This inference chain joins two existing models without training either one. Whisper converts the spoken request into text. A wrong transcription can change what is searched, so read the transcript before interpreting retrieval results. Where a reference transcript is available, WER counts changed, missing and extra words. CLIP then encodes the text query and compares it with gallery image vectors that have already been stored. Ranking returns the highest-scoring pictures. A failed result can come from the audio, transcription, text encoding or image ranking. Inspecting each intermediate output helps identify the cause instead of treating the whole chain as one unexplained error.
trace: The speaker says "a red car on a road".
If the transcript says "a red cart", search may change before CLIP runs.
Correct the query for a controlled comparison, then encode it once.
Compare the query with the stored gallery vectors and inspect the returned images.
diagrams.check_question: Which stage should you inspect first if the text query does not match the spoken words?
diagrams.check_answer: The speech transcript; CLIP is receiving the wrong query before image search begins.

A learned vector representing the content of an item.

A comparison of vector directions, independent of vector length.
Select a class by comparing descriptions, without training on that task's labels.
The fraction of the k returned results that are relevant.
Word substitutions, deletions and insertions divided by reference word count.
A projection that compresses vectors into fewer dimensions for inspection.

pitfalls: A high similarity score indicates model alignment, not proof that every detail in a query is present.
The lab's recall_at_k function computes precision@k; benchmark recall uses a different denominator.
A two-dimensional PCA plot discards information; visible distances do not fully describe the original embedding space.

recap.notes: Ask students to reconstruct the gallery search without reading the slide. Start with the text query and stored image vectors. Explain why the same learned comparison supports class-description matching and retrieval. Then ask which operations update weights: contrastive training can, but this lab uses frozen encoders. Revisit the three-pair matrix and the uniform-choice loss ln 3. Finish with the speech chain: an incorrect transcript gives CLIP an incorrect query. Use the exit question to distinguish precision from recall. A strong similarity score is one check, so students still inspect actual images, speech errors, data rights and performance across groups.
